The Age of Quirks.text: Generations ago, a baby was born in Qingqing City, China, glowing with a soft light. It was the first superhuman birth the world widely heard about, and within a few years similar reports came from everywhere. Children began manifesting powers that came to be called Quirks: flight, fire, extra limbs, strange senses. Laws, jobs, sports and insurance had all been built for ordinary bodies, and the old order cracked. Crime by people with powers grew faster than the police could answer it, governments struggled to keep control, and much of society's energy went into holding itself together. In that disorder some people used their powers to protect others with no legal right to do so. The state eventually answered with a system: Quirk registration, laws against public Quirk use and a licensed profession of heroes paid and regulated by the government. In Japan the Hero Public Safety Commission runs that system, and it has become the center of public life. Today about four in five people have a Quirk, and almost nobody alive remembers a world without them. Heroes are public servants, celebrities and the national ideal at once; children grow up with hero figures and ranking shows, and the hero academies are among the most competitive schools in the country. The chaotic early decades survive in textbooks and documentaries, and they remain the reason the rules exist: every restriction on Quirk use is the state's answer to the years when anyone with a dangerous power could do as they pleased.
